title: Bearing with others (I.16)
hook: bear with others' faults, since you have your own
tomorrow: what's sweet about a room where nothing happens?

segments.voice: Yesterday, temptation met at the door, while it's still only a knock, with a monk's book borrowing a love poet's line. The line was at the start.

Why put up with someone's worst habit? The Imitation gives an odd answer for a book about becoming holy. Whatever you can't fix in yourself or in someone else, it says, bear it patiently until God arranges things otherwise. Then it adds: maybe it's better that way. Better? This is a book that just spent pages on rooting out faults. Now it says some should be left standing, at least for a while. Why would a manual for improvement tell anyone to stop fixing a person?
screen: `BEAR WHAT YOU CAN'T FIX.` → `MAYBE IT'S BETTER THAT WAY?` → `WHY STOP FIXING A PERSON?`

segments.voice: Chapter sixteen of book one gives two reasons, and the second is the twist. First, patience. Without patience being tested, the book says, our good deeds don't weigh much. The friend who's always late is, among other things, a trainer. Annoying, and useful. Second, the mirror. Be patient with other people's faults, it says, because you have plenty that others have to put up with. If you can't make yourself the way you want to be, how can you expect someone else to be exactly to your liking? Then it catches us in the act. We want others perfect, and don't fix our own faults. We want them strictly corrected, and won't be corrected ourselves. So the puzzle solves itself: the habit you can't fix in someone else sits right next to one of yours that they can't fix either. And then the surprise. God set things up this way on purpose, the chapter says, so we'd learn to carry each other's loads, and it quotes Paul. In the Douay-Rheims: "Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ." Then the reason, in four short phrases: no one is without fault, no one without a burden, no one is enough for themselves, no one wise enough alone. Not a team of perfect people. A team of people carrying each other.
screen: `PATIENCE GIVES GOOD DEEDS WEIGHT.` · `YOU HAVE FAULTS TOO.` · `BEAR YE ONE ANOTHER'S BURDENS.` · `NO ONE IS ENOUGH ALONE.` · then, large: `YOU HAVE YOURS.`

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper, write one habit of someone else that wears on you. Underneath it, write one of your own that someone puts up with. Look at the two lines together for the rest of the sit, No need to fix either one yet. If you pray, ask for patience with both.
Bearing with others. The Imitation's counsel: be patient with other people's faults, since they're bearing with yours.
Hold onto this: you have yours, and somebody out there is carrying them with you. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1472 COUNTS.` → `THE IMITATION, READ THROUGH · 11 OF 30.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT'S SWEET ABOUT A ROOM WHERE NOTHING HAPPENS?`

howItsDone: Catholics count bearing wrongs patiently among the spiritual works of mercy, and religious communities in particular speak of mutual forbearance as part of daily life together.

options: Maybe both are true. Bear her lateness and own your bark; she's been carrying yours too.
No. The book says bear others' faults, so she should just bear your barking quietly.
